perspective:
Available to me, Harold Padilla:

- I am a project manager. I have a trusted friend/advisor, Arthur Begum, a police officer, and I often rely on him for advice and support.
- I felt frustrated and anxious because my project team seemed unmotivated and our progress was suffering. I arranged to meet Arthur at a coffee shop.
- I told Arthur my team seemed completely unmotivated and I was at my wit’s end. I heard Arthur say motivation can be tricky, ask whether I had tried understanding what drives each team member individually, advise that people need to feel valued and understood personally, and suggest one-on-one conversations. I admitted I had focused on goals and deadlines and said I would look into their personal motivations. I left feeling hopeful and relieved.
- I told my team we would have quick one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each of them. Team Member 1 said that could be helpful. Team Member 2 said they were open to it. I said I would schedule time with each of them and that we should make the project a success together.
- Later, I noticed the team still was not responding well and felt disappointed and worried about the project’s future. I told Arthur I had tried his suggestions but the team still was not responding. I heard Arthur say there may be deeper issues—personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors—and that I might need to dig deeper. I said I would set up another round of meetings.
- Determined and focused, I held one-on-one meetings. I told team members I had noticed performance issues and wanted to understand their concerns. Team Member 1 told me there was tension between a few people affecting work; I said I would look into resolving conflicts. Team Member 2 told me they felt overwhelmed by the workload and stressed; I said I understood and would see about redistributing tasks, and that their well-being was important.
- Feeling optimistic and empowered, I decided to create a more supportive, open team environment. I told the team we would have regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. Team Member 1 said that sounded great and would help us work better together. Team Member 2 agreed and said it was good that concerns were being addressed. I said I was glad and urged us to work together, emphasizing that their input and well-being were crucial to our success.

I do not have access to Arthur’s or team members’ private thoughts, hidden motives, or any events/information not listed above.
